title: Maximum Number of Jumps to Reach the Last Index
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` of length `n` (indexed from 0) and an integer `target`, and you start at index `0`. A single jump takes you from your current index `i` to any later index `j` (`i < j < n`) as long as the values differ by at most `target`, that is `|nums[j] - nums[i]| <= target`.

Return the largest number of jumps in any sequence of jumps that starts at index `0` and ends at index `n - 1`. If index `n - 1` cannot be reached at all, return `-1`.
notes:
## Intuition

Jumps only go forward, so the best way to arrive at index `j` depends only on the best ways to arrive at the earlier indices. Trying every jump sequence explodes exponentially, but the longest route to `j` is simply one more than the longest route to some earlier index `i` that can jump to `j`. That is a 1-D DP over the indices.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[j]` be the most jumps in a sequence from index 0 to index `j`, or `-1` if `j` cannot be reached. Start with `dp[0] = 0`.
2. For each `j` from 1 to `n - 1`, look at every earlier index `i`.
3. Skip `i` if it is unreachable (`dp[i] === -1`).
4. If `|nums[j] - nums[i]| <= target`, the jump `i → j` is allowed, so `dp[j]` can be `dp[i] + 1`; keep the maximum.
5. Return `dp[n - 1]`, which stays `-1` when the last index is unreachable.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,3,6,4,1,2]`, `target = 2`. `dp[0] = 0`. `dp[1] = 1` (from 0, difference 2). Index 2 (value 6) differs by 5 and 3 from the earlier values, so `dp[2] = -1`. `dp[3] = 2` (from index 1, difference 1). `dp[4] = 2` (from index 1, difference 2). For index 5 (value 2): from 0 gives 1, from 1 gives 2, from 3 gives 3, from 4 gives 3, so `dp[5] = 3`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): every pair `i < j` is checked once.
- Space: O(n) for `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- Never extend from an unreachable index: `-1 + 1 = 0` would wrongly make `j` reachable.
- The rule is on the absolute difference; a jump to a smaller value is allowed too.
- Values and `target` reach 2 · 10^9; in Java or C compute the difference in a 64-bit type to avoid overflow.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `nums` |
| `dp[j]` | most jumps from index 0 to index `j`, or `-1` if unreachable |
| `j` | index being reached |
| `i` | earlier index a jump to `j` could start from |

narration.3: dp[j] will hold the most jumps that land on j; -1 means j is not reachable yet.
narration.4: Index 0 is the start, reached with zero jumps.
narration.6: Fill dp from left to right, since jumps only go forward.
narration.7: Consider every earlier index i as the start of the last jump into j.
narration.8: An unreachable index cannot be the start of a jump.
narration.11: The jump from i to j is allowed only if the values differ by at most target.
narration.12: Landing on j through i costs one more jump than reaching i; keep the larger count.
narration.16: The answer is the best count for the last index, or -1 if it was never reached.
